To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) can be used to evaluate the relative quality of data for network inference, 2) conditioning-based similarity scores are superior to unpruned similarity scores, 3) the quality of the network inferences is mainly determined by the strength of the interactions in the network, and 4) steady-state data is informative enough to infer metabolic network structures.

(i) metabolic variations around steady state are sufficient to capture the topology of the underlying metabolic interactions, and (ii) the inference of metabolic network interactions from metabolomics data is a promising approach to study the underlying metabolic interactions.

the steady-state metabolome data are informative enough to infer the underlying metabolic network and that the Fisher information matrix is a useful measure to quantify the information quality of metabolomics data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a systematic analysis of the metabolic network inference problem and the information quality of the different data types.
the development of new approaches to analyze metabolic data and with the discovery of new insights into metabolic networks.
the development of a systematic approach for the reverse engineering of metabolic networks from metabolomics data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
steady state metabolic variations can be used for metabolic network inference, and that a proper selection of similarity measures is crucial for the success of this endeavor.
the metabolic network topology is well reflected in steady state metabolome data.
metabolic variations around steady state can be used as a source of information to infer the topology of the underlying metabolic interactions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a metabolic network can be reconstructed from metabolome data with a relatively low false-positive rate and a low computational cost, even if the data are generated from a single organism under steady state conditions.
metabolic networks can be inferred by analyzing steady-state metabolite data, and the quality of the data can be quantitatively evaluated to assess the reliability of the network inference.
the metabolic network topology can be inferred with a high confidence by using metabolome data obtained under slightly varying conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the inference of the underlying metabolic connectivity can be performed from a single organism at steady state, which is a rather simple experimental setup, with a low false discovery rate when appropriate statistical similarity scores are employed.

the information contained in the metabolome data is sufficient to reconstruct a metabolic network with a relatively high accuracy, which may have implications for the experimental design in the future.
metabolic variations observed around steady state can provide enough information to infer metabolic network connectivity, even in the absence of time series data.
